prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map separates the near machinery, bins, and floor—roughly 0.5–2 m from the camera wearer—from people and stacked materials generally about 2–6 m away, with walls and openings farther behind them. Across the five frames, the large machine remains directly in front and below the viewpoint while its nearer edges shift from centre-left to centre-right as the wearer turns; people move laterally through the mid-ground, but no clear large approach or retreat is resolved. Bright contours make object overlap and the limited space between the wearer, machine, and nearby workers clearer than RGB alone, including partially cropped foreground equipment along the lower edge. Metric distances, thin structures, people boundaries, and the bright floor/open doorway regions look unreliable because monocular depth is smooth, relative, and sometimes merges separate surfaces.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates multiple people distributed from far left to far right, usually about 2–6 m from the wearer, and shows when their silhouettes overlap or are partly cut off by frame boundaries; nearby pairs appear roughly 0.5–2 m apart. Across the strip, detections shift from a cluster on the left in frame 1, to people around the central machine in frames 2–3, and then to right-side figures in frames 4–5, clarifying lateral movement and occlusion even where clothing blends into the RGB background. The masks give clearer occupied image regions and relative left/right and above/below placement than RGB alone, but they do not independently establish depth, facing direction, gaze, or arm’s reach. Several labels are plainly unreliable in context—small regions marked “car,” “kite,” or “umbrella” correspond to workshop structures or occluded items—and some visible people and objects are missed or incompletely masked.
descriptions.pose: The pose map recovers only three body skeletons: one low-left in frame 1, one near the centre of frame 3, and one low-right in frame 5, corresponding roughly to people about 2–5 m from the wearer; no reliable hand skeletons are visible. Their joint layouts show body orientation more clearly than RGB alone: the first appears side-on and bent or leaning, the middle figure is upright with the torso turned obliquely, and the last is bent forward or sideways, but head keypoints are insufficient to confirm gaze toward the wearer. The skeletons also expose limb height and reach relative to nearby surfaces, although none is shown close enough to establish that the camera wearer could reach them, while each detected person’s own arms appear within reach of adjacent equipment or objects. Most people receive no pose at all, several limbs are missing or compressed by foreshortening and occlusion, and the sparse detections make apparent changes across frames unreliable as continuous approach, retreat, or turning.
